newsitem.title: UK: SOCCER-EMOTIONAL AFTERNOON AHEAD AT HIGHBURY AND STAMFORD BRIDGE.
newsitem.headline: SOCCER-EMOTIONAL AFTERNOON AHEAD AT HIGHBURY AND STAMFORD BRIDGE.

text.p: The absence of one man and the presence of another will make the atmosphere at the two biggest matches in London on Saturday even more highly-charged than usual.

The tragic death of 42-year-old Chelsea vice-chairman Matthew Harding has left a painful void at Stamford Bridge where Tottenham are the visitors for the premier league derby that down the years has provided plenty of emotion and drama in its own right.
Saturday's match, overshadowed by Harding's death in a helicopter crash on Wednesday night, will be played against a background of deep sorrow.

The match was already a sell-out before Harding died, but with the players wearing black armbands, a minute's silence due to be held before kickoff, and with Harding's widow and four children expected to attend, the result is almost of secondary importance to the occasion.

Tottenham offered to postpone the match as a mark of respect, but Chelsea said they wanted the game played and with Ruud Gullit expected to return for his first full league match of the season, nothing less than three points will do for the home side.
Across London at Highbury, the atmosphere will be charged not for the poignant absence of a man, but for one man's poignant return.

George Graham goes back to Highbury as an opponent for the first time since leaving Arsenal where he won six major trophies in eight years before being fired for his part in an illegal payments scandal.
Graham was banned from the game for a year after leaving Arsenal and spent 20 months out of football before taking over as manager from Howard Wilkinson at ailing Leeds five weeks ago.

Since then, his injury-hit team have lost four out of five league games, slipped from 12th to 16th in the table, and on Wednesday night went out of the League Cup in a repeat of last season's Wembley final against Aston Villa at Elland Road.
It might be suspected that Graham, even if he cannot win another game this season, would be happy just to beat Arsenal but he says: "That's not the case at all.
"I've come to Leeds because I was yearning to return to football with a club of such great potential where I believe I can build success long-term like I had at Highbury.
"I'm looking forward to going back to Highbury. I had 15 years there as a player and manager and they were full of mostly happy memories.
"I will always have a great deal of affection for the club -- and especially for the players I brought in, many of whom are still there and still performing superbly."
Arsenal have offered the hand of friendship to Graham with chairman Peter Hill-Wood inviting Graham to share a post-match drink in the boardroom.

Hill-Wood said: "It's time to leave differences aside and put the past behind us. Visiting managers often come up to the boardroom for a drink after the match. If George does, he will be most welcome."
In terms of this week's tragedy at Chelsea, Graham's misdemeanours pale into insignificance.
He might well have a drink in the Arsenal boardroom where the only appropriate toast would be to "absent friends."
